"The Drug War Backfires," The New York Times Says

(Marijuananews note: There is no mention of marijuana in this editorial, but they are not yet ready to confront that issue. The Times will try for the "conservative" position that the Drug War was just a "failure." That way, no one is to blame. Interestingly, it uses the word Prohibition in the first sentence, but only as an analogy. It does not use it again to refer directly to the present policies, but it is inescapable.

Of course, any criticism of prohibition at this level is a major challenge to the solidarity of the party line. Prohibitionism is too brittle to give an inch. It will hold until it breaks, but this is a serious blow.

Notice the heretical remarks by the Drug Czar. He is clearly looking for an exit strategy. Every General for himself!)


THE DRUG WAR BACKFIRES
See
New York Times Derides Summit As "Cheerleaders" Who "recycle unrealistic pledges and celebrate dubious programs."

Of course, any criticism of prohibition at this level is a major challenge to the solidarity of the party line. Prohibitionism is too brittle to give an inch. It will hold until it breaks, but this is a serious blow.

Notice the heretical remarks by the Drug Czar. He is clearly looking for an exit strategy. Every General for himself!)

March 13, 1999
From The New York Times
Editorial
letters@nytimes.com
http://www.nytimes.com/
http://forums.nytimes.com/comment/

Almost 70 years after the failure of Prohibition

The boomerang effect of the failed policy

School systems deteriorate while tax dollars build new prisons. Municipal police forces have grown so militarized that drug warrants are served in armored personnel carriers. Young mothers are imprisoned for years for simple drug possession. Young black males in California are now five times as likely to go to prison as to a state university.

The drug war was created in reaction to a wave of urban violence triggered by crack cocaine that ignited fears that crack addiction might spread widely. Surveys now show, however, that the use of crack, by about 600,000 people annually, has not changed in 10 years. Nor has the general level of illegal drug use.

The best hope for controlling illicit drugs lies in treatment. Unfortunately, as new prisons have gone up, treatment programs within them have declined. In their obsession to control drug use by making war on it, Federal and state legislators have turned the world’s greatest democracy into its largest prison system, where young adults are warehoused and the opportunity to treat them is wasted.

As General McCaffrey says, "we can’t incarcerate our way out of this problem." But we can, he argues, focus punishment on drug dealers, not drug users, while beginning to treat the hundreds of thousands of people in prison with drug problems.

(Marijuananews note: Perestroika was intended just to make Communism work, so one gets the impression that the logical conclusion toward which this editorial was moving was literally cut off at the end.)
